issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
Kwame is a 62-year-old married African American man who has spent the better part of four decades as a bomb disposal technician - a career built on precision, composure, and the willingness to walk toward danger that others run from. He presented for psychological assessment following increasing concern from his wife and his unit supervisor, both of whom had noticed a marked deterioration in his functioning over the preceding eighteen months. His PCL-5 score of 57 places him firmly in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a man whose professional identity had become both a refuge and a trap.

The precipitating event occurred approximately two years ago during a routine inspection of a suspected improvised device at an industrial site. What appeared to be a standard render-safe procedure became something else entirely when Kwame detected an unexpected chemical odour - sharp, synthetic, nothing he could immediately classify - seconds before a partial detonation released a cloud of toxic gas. He was evacuated and hospitalised for eleven days. The ward smelled of antiseptic and machinery. Nurses moved quickly around him. Alarms sounded at intervals he could not predict. He was told, at one point, that had he been standing two feet closer, the exposure would have been fatal. He was discharged with a clean bill of physical health, and he returned to work within six weeks. He told no one that anything was wrong.

The symptoms announced themselves gradually. Back at the disposal unit, the ambient smells of the workplace - industrial solvents, metalwork, the particular chemical tang of protective equipment - began to carry something they had not carried before. On two occasions in his first month back, Kwame found himself frozen at his workstation, heart hammering, certain that he was again breathing something toxic. The hospital smell - antiseptic, sterile, faintly sweet - became equally unbearable; a routine physical examination eight months after the incident triggered such acute distress that he left the clinic before it was completed, and he has not returned since. Loud, sudden noises - a dropped canister, a vehicle backfiring in the yard - produced an immediate, full-body alarm response that he found humiliating and impossible to explain to younger colleagues. These sensory triggers reliably activated a state of heightened threat perception that, once switched on, was very difficult to switch off. He would spend the remainder of those shifts scanning the room continuously, cataloguing exit points, tracking the movements of everyone around him, his body certain that whatever had nearly killed him once was still present, still circling.

What Kwame had come to believe - quietly, without ever articulating it clearly - was that the world had become genuinely less safe, and that his survival depended on his own vigilance. He began mapping exits as a matter of course, in the canteen, in briefing rooms, at church. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a colleague once caused him to spin around with enough force to alarm the man who had touched him. This persistent state of readiness fed back into the triggers themselves: because he was always scanning, he was always finding things - a smell, a sound, a visual detail - that confirmed his suspicion that danger was near, and the cycle tightened.

The strategies Kwame developed to manage this were logical to him, if costly. He began volunteering for every available shift, arriving early and staying late, filling every hour with the structured demands of work so that he would never be left alone in a room with his own thoughts. He avoided being at home alone. He refused all medical appointments. But the overwork, paradoxical as it was, kept him embedded in the very environment - the workplace smells, the sudden noises, the physical proximity of colleagues who might brush against him - that sustained his threat monitoring. His hypervigilance, fed by constant re-exposure, never fully subsided.

What finally brought Kwame to the clinic was his wife's ultimatum, delivered quietly one evening after he had slept, for the fourth consecutive night, in his car rather than come inside to an empty house. He arrived presenting as controlled and somewhat reluctant. What he feared most, he said near the end of the first session, was that if he stopped working, stopped moving, stopped watching - something would get through.
